The turn-resolved prediction of the six stored PF coils puts PF2's first open winding mode at 595 Hz (pre-test frequency response). That is 0.8 % below 600 Hz, the twelve-pulse line its three thyristor units make above 22 kA. Its VS1 carrier at 500 Hz sits 19 % below the mode. PF5's first open mode, 276 Hz, is 8 % below 300 Hz. Each unit makes that six-pulse line from 5.5 to 22 kA, where it fires one bridge. No other PF coil has a mode within 15 % of a line it carries.

A converter line that lands on a winding mode is amplified inside the winding. The terminals do not show it, so the voltage stress studies done so far, which judge terminals and the first turns, would not either. The amplification is set by the mode's damping, and that is the unknown. The ladder that found the modes is loss-free. Its poles have no width, so it cannot say whether the gain at 600 Hz is 1.2 or 20. The frequency is uncertain too. On PF6, the one coil with a measured sweep, the model's first tied mode is at least 15 % below the measured one. If PF2's open mode is low by the same amount, it sits near 690 Hz, well clear of 600 Hz. If it is not, it sits on the line.

The PF6 damping study already bounds an installed first-mode quality factor of 0.60–0.89, with the TF case's share limited by passivity (PF winding damping). If PF2 and PF5 damp alike, the coincidence is harmless. This plan finds out, and says which measurement would settle it if the bounds cannot.

§1 — The modes' frequency band and damping, stored and installed

Run the damping method of scripts/iter/winding_damping.py on PF2 and PF5 through their owners: turn_resolved_coil and pf_turn_layout in src/power_convertor/coil_windings.py, and coil_coupling.capacitance_nodal. Bound the quality factor of the first three modes at 293 K stored and at 4 K installed, with the TF-case share capped at the passivity ceiling as for PF6. The script's driver serves PF1 and PF6 only today: main() raises unless its source coil is PF6 and loops over PF6 and PF1. This section makes the coil an argument of that driver, so that PF2 and PF5 run through the same functions, and the PF1 and PF6 outputs stay unchanged. That coil parameter, and one --coil flag beside the existing --check-zero-loss and --stress-figure-only, are the whole added surface; nothing is retired, because the driver keeps serving PF1 and PF6 by default. Give each mode a frequency band. The low end is the model value. The high end is the model value raised by the PF6 tied-mode discrepancy, a factor of at least 1.17, unless a PF2- or PF5-specific measurement says otherwise. That factor is the measured first tied mode's lower bound, 2 kHz from YVUELA's sweep as the pre-test frequency response record states it, over the model's first tied mode, 1,708 Hz, which coil_record in scripts/iter/frequency_response_prediction.py returns as PF6's first shorted_resonances_hz. Compute it from coil_record and that stated bound, as one named constant, and state both inputs in the record. The extended driver writes the band and Q table; there is no second entry point. The record is docs/research/iter-pf-winding-line-resonance.html. Figures go in docs/figures/iter-pf-winding-line-resonance/.

Done when PF2's and PF5's first three modes each have a frequency band and a Q interval for both states, and the record states whether 600 Hz (PF2) and 300 Hz (PF5) lie inside the band. Positive control: PF6 run through the same call reproduces the PF6 damping study's Q intervals to their stated digits. Negative control: with every loss removed, the reported Q interval grows without bound, showing that the bound comes from the losses and not from the method.

§2 — The converter lines driven through the winding

Drive the damped, turn-resolved PF2 winding with its three switched thyristor units and its VS1 IGBT units. The drive already exists: simulate_window in scripts/iter/pf_switched_pulse.py builds the turn-resolved winding through ConverterNetwork, spreads the plasma's and the other coils' flux through add_prescribed_winding_sources, picks windows with choose_instants, whose near-90° rule is the window this section needs, and measures lines with line_peak. It takes the coil as an argument and runs undamped. This section adds the damping and the band corner as arguments of simulate_window and its CLI, with no second driver. Use the scenario windows where PF2's 600 Hz line is largest, from the scenario loading intervals over the SRO cases, and drive PF5 the same way in its one-bridge band. Run each window at both ends of §1's frequency band and Q interval. Take the internal peaks from scripts/iter/exterior_turn_voltages.py (peak_to_ground, neighbour_peak, turn_to_turn_peak), and the insulation reference from TURN_TO_TURN_CRITERION_V in src/power_convertor/coil_windings.py, whose comment records that no PF winding has a specified impulse test.

Report, per coil and arm:

  • the internal voltage amplitude at the line frequency (600 Hz for PF2, 300 Hz for PF5) to ground, between adjacent turns and between adjacent pancakes. The largest time-domain peaks are reported beside it as edge content. With ideal switches their edges are instantaneous and the peaks do not converge with the step; they converge only with a finite edge rate, which is iter-switched-terminal-transients §7's question;
  • the amplification at the line, as the ratio of the internal peak to the peak the same terminal drive gives on a winding with its first mode moved 30 % away;
  • the margin of each peak against the coil's insulation test level, cited from the IDM register or marked undocumented.

Done when that table is complete at all four band corners for both coils. Positive control: a single lumped RLC with §1's mode and Q, driven by the same line amplitude, reproduces the analytic resonant gain within 2 %. Negative control: on the detuned winding, the ratio of the internal peak to the terminal peak at the line is within 10 % of the same ratio for a drive at one tenth of the line frequency, showing that moving the mode removes the resonant gain, or the record explains why it is not. The solver step is halved once, and no reported line amplitude may move by more than 2 %. With damping and band arguments at their defaults, simulate_window reproduces its current undamped PF1/PF6 outputs.

Re-measured on the converged, lossy winding

The verdict above was set on the turn-resolved winding with a modal Q. The winding has since become the converged library winding with cited cold installed losses (WindingLosses) and effective-turn linkage, so the reopened measurement runs on that winding, not on the turn-resolved one, and carries the losses at both installed-loss bounds instead of the modal-Q corners. Done when, for PF2 at 600 Hz and PF5 at 300 Hz, the loaded-to-detuned internal line ratio is reported at both bounds, to ground and between adjacent sections, from paired switched replays whose terminal-line ratio stays within 1 % of unity. Where the terminal ratio leaves that band, the internal ratio is normalised by it, and the record says so. Negative control: replaying with the losses removed raises the internal ratio above the lossy value at the upper bound, so the losses are shown to act. The earlier modal-Q replay path is not accepted as evidence for this measurement.

§3 — The measurement that settles it

Where §2's verdict depends on where the band falls, name the test that removes the dependence. Give the coil, its state, the sweep range and resolution, and the quantity that decides it: the first open mode's frequency within ±3 % and its Q within a factor of two. Write it as an addition to the frequency-response request, which today covers the stored PF1 and PF3 coils. The lead decides whether it is sent.

Done when the record states, for each coil, whether the coincidence is a finding against the IDM insulation levels, a bounded non-issue, or open pending the named measurement, with the deciding number beside it. Where a coil is open, the request addition names its sweep range, resolution and deciding quantity. Negative control: a coil whose band §2 found clear of its line at every corner is classed as a bounded non-issue and gets no request entry.

§4 — The PF2 transformer-phase lever

Measure the one converter-side lever. PF2's three series units can be fired with their transformers at different phases. The PF1/PF6 interunit study showed that equal angles on two units drop the 600 Hz line by 22.9 dB, while sequential control moves it with the two angles (PF1 and PF6 interunit phase comparison). Report what the documented PF2 transformer phases and sequential law do to PF2's 600 Hz line over §2's windows. Extend the phase study that already lives in scripts/iter/pf_switched_pulse.py (UNIT_PHASES_DEG, PHASE_STUDY_OUTPUT, the --arm flag whose choices come from UNIT_PHASES_DEG and reach the solver as simulate_window(unit_phases_deg=...)) with PF2's three units, rather than writing a second study. Do not propose a new phase arrangement. IDM decides that. This section needs §2's windows and runs beside §3.

Done when the record states PF2's 600 Hz line, in volts and in decibels against the in-phase arrangement, for each of §2's windows under the documented phases and sequential law. Positive control: the same code, applied to the PF1/PF6 loaded pair with both units at 105°, reproduces the interunit study's 22.9 dB drop of the 600 Hz line within 1 dB. Negative control: with the interunit displacement set to zero, the same code restores the 600 Hz line to the in-phase 361.11 V within 1 dB.
